tagline: A prophetic poem announcing the fall of Nineveh, capital of the Assyrian empire, and the end of its long cruelty toward the nations.
overview:
Nahum is a single, sustained oracle against one city. Nineveh, on the Tigris River in what is now northern Iraq, was the capital of Assyria, the empire that had dominated the Near East for more than a century, destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel, and ravaged Judah. Nahum announces that God is about to bring that city down. The book opens with a hymn to the LORD as a jealous and avenging God who is also slow to anger and a stronghold for those who trust in him, then turns to vivid battle poetry: chariots racing through the streets, river gates thrown open, treasure plundered, and the lion's den of Assyria left empty.

The book is short, fierce, and poetically brilliant, and it unsettles many modern readers because it celebrates the downfall of a people. It helps to read it as its first audience did. For Judah, Assyria was not an abstract enemy but the power that had deported their relatives, besieged their cities, and boasted in its inscriptions of flaying and impaling its victims. Nahum is a word of comfort to the oppressed: the empire that seemed permanent will fall, because the God of Israel rules the nations and does not leave the guilty unpunished.

Nahum also forms a counterpart to Jonah. In Jonah, Nineveh repents and God spares it, to the prophet's dismay. In Nahum, a later Nineveh has returned to violence and faces judgment. Read together, the two books show both sides of God's character revealed at Sinai: compassion that relents when people turn, and justice that will not leave oppression unanswered forever.
author: The book names its author only as Nahum the Elkoshite (1:1). The name means comfort, which fits the book's message to Judah. Nothing else is known of him, and the location of Elkosh is uncertain. Proposals include a site in Galilee, a village in southern Judah, and Al Qosh near Mosul in northern Iraq, where a tradition of Nahum's tomb survives; none can be confirmed. Scholars generally accept that the poetry comes from a single gifted writer, though some think the opening hymn (1:2-8) was an existing psalm adapted for its place at the head of the book.
date: The book must have been written after the fall of Thebes in Egypt, which it mentions as a past event (3:8-10). The Assyrian king Ashurbanipal sacked Thebes around 663 BC. It speaks of Nineveh's fall as still to come, and Nineveh fell in 612 BC. Within that window, some scholars place Nahum soon after 663, when the memory of Thebes was fresh and Assyria was at its height; others prefer a date closer to 612, when Assyria was visibly weakening after Ashurbanipal's death and the rise of Babylon. A minority of critical scholars have argued that some of the poetry was written after the event, but most read it as genuine prediction or anticipation.
setting: Assyria's power in the seventh century BC was immense. Its kings, including Sennacherib, Esarhaddon, and Ashurbanipal, ruled from the Persian Gulf to Egypt, and Sennacherib had made Nineveh a magnificent capital with palaces, gardens, and an aqueduct. Judah under King Manasseh (about 697 to 642 BC) was an Assyrian vassal, paying tribute. After Ashurbanipal's death (dated by scholars to the 630s or 620s BC), the empire weakened quickly. The Babylonians under Nabopolassar rebelled, and in 612 BC a coalition of Babylonians and Medes besieged and destroyed Nineveh, an event recorded in the Babylonian Chronicle. The last Assyrian resistance, at Harran, collapsed by 609 BC, and the Egyptian army that had come to Assyria's aid was defeated by Babylon at Carchemish in 605 BC. Within a generation, the empire Nahum describes had vanished, and Nineveh lay in ruins until its rediscovery by archaeologists in the nineteenth century.
purpose: Nahum was written to comfort Judah and to declare the justice of God. For a people who had lived for generations under Assyrian domination, the book announces that the yoke will be broken (1:13) and that the one who brings good news of peace is on the mountains (1:15). It also teaches that no empire is beyond God's reach. Assyria's gods, armies, and wealth could not protect it, because the LORD, not Assyria, governs history. The book invites Judah to trust the God who is a stronghold in the day of distress and to celebrate its feasts again in freedom.
story: Nahum stands among the twelve Minor Prophets, between Micah and Habakkuk. In the Bible's larger story, Assyria has been the great threat since the days of Hosea, Amos, Isaiah, and Micah: it destroyed Samaria in 722 BC and nearly took Jerusalem in 701 BC. Jonah had shown God's willingness to spare even Nineveh. Nahum shows the end of Assyria's story, and in doing so prepares for the next chapter, in which Babylon, the power that toppled Nineveh, becomes the rod of God's judgment on Judah (the subject of Habakkuk). The pattern Nahum traces, a proud empire exalting itself and then falling, recurs through Daniel and reaches its final form in Revelation's vision of the fall of Babylon the great.
christ: Nahum is not a book of messianic prophecy, and its links to Christ are thematic rather than predictive. Its announcement of the one who brings good news of peace (1:15) closely parallels Isaiah 52:7, which Paul quotes in Romans 10:15 to describe those who preach the gospel. Its picture of God as a warrior who breaks the yoke of the oppressor anticipates the New Testament's confidence that Christ has disarmed the powers and will one day judge the world in righteousness. Revelation's lament over the fall of Babylon the great, with its merchants, its sorceries, and its seduction of the nations, echoes Nahum's taunt against Nineveh (Nahum 3:4, Revelation 18). And the book's insistence that God will by no means leave the guilty unpunished finds its most surprising answer at the cross, where God's justice against sin is carried out in a way that also opens the door to mercy for Nineveh's descendants and for all nations.
reading: Nahum is poetry, and very good poetry: rapid, visual, full of sound and motion. Read it aloud. Its genre is the oracle against a foreign nation, a form found in many prophets (Isaiah 13 to 23, Jeremiah 46 to 51, Amos 1 to 2), and like those oracles it was spoken for the ears of God's people, not delivered to the foreign city. Watch for the book's structure: a hymn about God's character (chapter 1), a battle vision (chapter 2), and a taunt song with a woe (chapter 3). A common misreading is to take the book as endorsing hatred of enemies or national gloating. The book's subject is God's justice on a specific, violent empire, and its opening hymn insists that God is slow to anger and good to those who trust him. Reading Nahum alongside Jonah, and remembering the suffering Assyria inflicted, helps keep both God's justice and his mercy in view.

structure.title: The LORD, avenger and refuge
structure.summary: A hymn, partly shaped as an alphabetic acrostic, describing God's power over nature and his judgment on enemies, and his care for those who trust him.

structure.title: Judgment for Nineveh, relief for Judah
structure.summary: Oracles alternate between Nineveh's doom and Judah's release from the yoke, ending with the messenger of peace on the mountains.

structure.title: The attack on Nineveh
structure.summary: A vivid picture of the assault: red shields, flashing chariots, opened river gates, plunder, and the empty den of the Assyrian lion.

structure.title: Woe to the city of blood
structure.summary: A taunt song exposing Nineveh's violence and seduction, comparing it to fallen Thebes, and ending with its incurable wound and the world's applause.

themes.title: The justice of God
themes.body: Nahum insists that God does not ignore oppression. The phrase that the LORD will by no means leave the guilty unpunished comes from God's self-revelation in Exodus 34:7, and the book applies it to an empire that had built its wealth on plunder and terror. God's justice is not a mood but his faithful commitment to set right what the powerful have made wrong.

themes.title: God's rule over the nations
themes.body: Assyria seemed unstoppable, yet the book presents its fall as the LORD's decision. Rivers, mountains, and armies obey him. No empire, however great, stands outside his government, and no ruler can claim ultimate authority over the peoples of the earth.

themes.title: Comfort for the oppressed
themes.body: The prophet's name means comfort, and the book is addressed to a people who had suffered under Assyria for generations. God promises to break their yoke and tear away their shackles, and to let them celebrate their feasts in peace. Judgment on the oppressor is good news for the oppressed.

themes.title: The emptiness of violent power
themes.body: Nineveh is pictured as a lion's den filled with prey, a city of blood full of lies and plunder. Its end shows the self-defeating nature of power built on cruelty: the city that terrified others becomes a spectacle, and no one mourns it.

keyChapters.why: The hymn to God's character sets the terms for the book: a jealous, avenging God who is also slow to anger, good, and a stronghold for those who trust him.
The poetic description of Nineveh's fall, with its river gates, plunder, and empty lion's den, is among the most vivid battle poetry in the Bible.
The woe against the city of blood and the comparison with Thebes explain why Nineveh falls, and the book's closing question leaves the reader weighing the cost of cruelty.

parts.body:
Nahum is the seventh of the twelve shorter prophets, three chapters long. It is a single, sustained word against one city: Nineveh, on the Tigris in what is now northern Iraq, the capital of Assyria. Assyria had ruled the Near East for more than a century, destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel and ravaged Judah. Nahum announces that God is about to bring that city down.

The book opens with a hymn to the LORD, ‘a jealous and avenging God’ (1:2), who is also ‘slow to anger and great in power’ (1:3) and ‘a stronghold in the day of distress’ (1:7). Then it turns to battle poetry: chariots racing through the streets, river gates thrown open, treasure carried off, and the lion's den of Assyria left empty.

The book unsettles many readers because it seems to celebrate the fall of a people. It helps to read it as its first hearers did. For Judah, Assyria was the power that had deported their relatives and besieged their cities. Nahum is a word of comfort to the oppressed: the empire that seemed permanent will fall, because the God of Israel rules the nations and does not leave the guilty unpunished.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Nahum is a counterpart to Jonah. In Jonah, Nineveh repents and God spares it, to the prophet's dismay. In Nahum, a later Nineveh has returned to violence and faces judgment. Read together, the two books show both sides of God's character as he made it known at Sinai: compassion that relents when people turn, and justice that will not leave oppression unanswered for ever. The canon keeps them together in the one Book of the Twelve.

Both books end with a question. Jonah ends with God asking whether he should not care about Nineveh. Nahum ends by asking who has not felt Nineveh's cruelty.

The book names its author only as ‘Nahum the Elkoshite’ (1:1). The name means comfort, which fits its message to Judah. Nothing else is known of him, and where Elkosh lay is uncertain. Proposals include a site in Galilee, a village in southern Judah, and Al Qosh near Mosul in northern Iraq, where a tradition of Nahum's tomb survives; none can be confirmed. Scholars generally accept that the poetry comes from one gifted writer, though some think the opening hymn was an existing psalm adapted for its place.

The book must come after the fall of Thebes in Egypt, which it mentions as past (3:8-10). The Assyrian king Ashurbanipal sacked Thebes around 663 BC. It speaks of Nineveh's fall as still to come, and Nineveh fell in 612 BC. Within that window, some scholars place Nahum soon after 663, when the memory of Thebes was fresh and Assyria at its height; others prefer a date near 612, when Assyria was weakening. The site's guide to the kings agrees on the window, between 663 and 612, and says that Nahum probably spoke in Josiah's reign. A minority of critical scholars think some of the poetry was written after the event; most read it as real prediction.

Assyria's power in the seventh century BC was immense. Its kings, Sennacherib, Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal among them, ruled from the Persian Gulf to Egypt, and Sennacherib had made Nineveh a magnificent capital with palaces, gardens and an aqueduct. Judah under Manasseh was an Assyrian vassal, paying tribute. Assyrian royal art lined the palaces of Nineveh with carved stone scenes of the king's campaigns: siege ramps, burning cities, captives led away. Many are now in the British Museum, among them Sennacherib's siege of Lachish in Judah.

After Ashurbanipal's death, which scholars date to the 630s or 620s BC, the empire weakened quickly. The Babylonians under Nabopolassar rebelled, and in 612 BC Babylonians and Medes besieged and destroyed Nineveh, an event recorded in the Babylonian Chronicle. The last Assyrian resistance, at Harran, collapsed by 609 BC, and the Egyptian army that came to Assyria's aid was defeated by Babylon at Carchemish in 605 BC. Within a generation the empire Nahum describes was gone, and Nineveh lay in ruins until archaeologists found it again in the nineteenth century.

The book has three parts. Chapter 1 is a hymn about God's character, followed by words that turn back and forth between Nineveh and Judah, ending with a messenger running over the mountains with news of peace. Chapter 2 is a vision of battle. Chapter 3 is a taunt song that opens with a woe.

Nahum is poetry, and very good poetry: rapid, full of sound and motion. Read it aloud. Its form is the prophet's word against a foreign nation, found in many prophets, and like those words it was spoken for the ears of God's people, not delivered to the foreign city.

parts.h: A jealous and avenging God, slow to anger
parts.body:
‘The LORD is a jealous and avenging God; the LORD is avenging and full of wrath’ (1:2). Many readers are uncomfortable with a God who takes vengeance, and the book's notes give several ways of understanding it. In the Bible vengeance is a legal idea, the act of a just ruler who defends the wronged and punishes the wrongdoer, not the spite of a wounded ego. The chapter balances wrath with patience and goodness: ‘The LORD is slow to anger and great in power’ (1:3), and ‘The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of distress; He cares for those who trust in Him’ (1:7). And the object of God's wrath is an empire known from its own records for mass deportation, torture and plunder. A God indifferent to that would not be good.

Some readers still find the intensity of the language troubling, and note that the Bible holds a wider picture, including God's mercy to Nineveh in Jonah. Others say that Assyria's victims would have heard Nahum's words as the long-awaited assurance that their suffering mattered to God. Both responses take the text seriously.

The chapter ends with a runner on the mountains, ‘the feet of one who brings good news, who proclaims peace’ (1:15). The oppressor will never again march through Judah.

Chapter 2 is some of the most vivid battle poetry in the Old Testament. An attacker advances, and the prophet mockingly tells Nineveh to man its walls. Red shields and scarlet uniforms, chariots flashing like torches, the river gates opened, the palace melting away, the treasure carried off. Then a taunt: where is the lions' den? Assyrian kings described themselves as lions and staged lion hunts as displays of power, and the royal lion had hauled prey home to its cubs. Now the den is empty. ‘Behold, I am against you,’ declares the LORD of Hosts (2:13).

Chapter 3 opens, ‘Woe to the city of blood, full of lies, full of plunder, never without prey’ (3:1). Nineveh is pictured as a seductive woman and a sorceress who trapped nations in alliances that became chains. Then a question: ‘Are you better than Thebes’ (3:8)? Assyria had done to Thebes everything Nineveh now faces. The book ends with the king of Assyria told that his wound is incurable, and that all who hear of his fall will clap their hands, ‘for who has not experienced your constant cruelty?’ (3:19).

parts.h: Reading a book about an enemy's fall
parts.body:
The poetry of Nahum does not pause to mourn Nineveh, and that troubles many readers. Several things help. The book is written from the side of Assyria's victims, who had suffered exactly these things at Assyrian hands, and Assyria's own carvings celebrate burning cities and deported captives. It shows the terrible logic of violence coming home. It gives the judgment to God and never invites Judah to take revenge. The prophets elsewhere show grief even over enemy nations, and Jonah records God's compassion for Nineveh's people and animals. God asks in Ezekiel, ‘Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked?’ (Ezekiel 18:23).

So these notes do not gloat, and they do not invite readers to. The cruelties the book names, at Thebes and at Nineveh, are named here and not described. Nineveh's fall is no key for reading any people's suffering, then or now, as a punishment they deserved, and no warrant for anyone to wish destruction on a city or a people today. The picture of Nineveh as a shamed woman in 3:5 is a picture of a city's disgrace, drawn from the prophets' vocabulary of humiliation. It gives no warrant for shaming or harming any woman.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Nahum
parts.body:
The New Testament never quotes Nahum, and these notes draw no line it does not draw.

The good news on the mountains in 1:15 closely matches Isaiah 52:7, ‘How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news’ (Isaiah 52:7), and it is Isaiah's form that Paul quotes when he speaks of those sent to preach (Romans 10:15).

Read Nahum aloud, and let its speed and noise land. Read it beside Jonah, and keep both God's mercy and his justice in view.

Read it from the side of the oppressed, for whom it was written. It says that no empire is permanent, that God sees what the powerful do to the weak, and that their suffering matters to him. Read it as a warning to every power that trusts in violence, including any the reader belongs to, before it is a comfort against anyone else.

And let its last question stay with you. Who has not experienced your constant cruelty? Ask who could say that of you.

hard.line: A jealous and avenging God: vengeance as the act of a just ruler, set beside slow to anger and good.
Good news on the mountains, and the oppressor cut off.
The plunder of a city told without mourning: written from the side of Assyria's victims.
Nineveh pictured as a shamed woman: a city's disgrace, no warrant to shame any woman.
The sack of Thebes, which Assyria itself had done: named, not described.
The book ends with applause at Nineveh's fall and no offer of mercy, unlike Jonah.

words.line: Assyria's capital on the Tigris, which fell in 612 BC (1:1; 2:8; 3:7).
Massa, a heading for a prophet's word against a nation (1:1).
Nahum's home, Elkosh, whose place is uncertain (1:1).
God's zeal for his people and his own name, which will not share them with rivals (1:2).
Vengeance as a legal act: a just ruler defending the wronged (1:2).
God's patience, from his words to Moses at Sinai, set in the middle of the hymn (1:3).
God as a refuge for those who trust him in the day of trouble (1:7).
The runner on the mountains proclaiming peace (1:15).
Assyria pictured as a lion that hauled prey home, now empty (2:11-12).
Hoy, the funeral cry, raised over the city of blood (3:1).
No-Amon, the great Egyptian city on the Nile that Assyria sacked around 663 BC (3:8).

timeline.what: Sennacherib invades Judah and besieges Jerusalem (2 Kings 18 to 19). His palace at Nineveh shows the siege of Lachish.
Manasseh reigns in Judah as an Assyrian vassal.
Ashurbanipal of Assyria sacks Thebes in Egypt, which Nahum names as past (3:8-10).
Nahum speaks, probably in Josiah's reign by the site's guide to the kings; some scholars prefer soon after 663, others near 612.
Ashurbanipal dies, as scholars date it, and Assyria weakens quickly.
Babylonians and Medes destroy Nineveh, as the Babylonian Chronicle records.
Assyria's last stand at Harran collapses (609); Babylon defeats Egypt at Carchemish (605).

map.title: Judah, who heard Nahum's good news

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: Judah's capital, drawn to mark Judah, whom Nahum tells to keep its feasts because the oppressor is cut off (1:15). Nahum names Judah, not the city.

teaching.mapNote: Only Jerusalem is drawn, at the point this site's maps use, to mark Judah. Nineveh, Thebes, Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon are left off, because they are not placed in this site's records, and so are Egypt, Cush, Put and Libya. No borders are drawn. The map makes no claim about any border today.
